deep.reconstruction:
There is no mathematics on this page. It is a philosophical draft, a critical discussion of Gustav Theodor Fechner's natural philosophy. The argument runs as follows.

(1) In 'Nanna' (1848, on the soul-life of plants) Fechner argues that plants have souls. In 'Zend-Avesta' (1851) his starting point is the doctrine that the heavenly bodies have souls.

(2) Riemann characterises Fechner's method. It is not the scientific method of abstracting general laws by induction and then applying and testing them in the explanation of nature. It is analogy. Fechner compares the Earth with our own organism, which we know to be ensouled. He weighs similarities and differences fairly and concludes:
- the similarities show that the Earth is an ensouled being;
- the differences show that it is a far higher ensouled being than we are.

(3) Riemann's assessment: the persuasive force of this lies in the vivid, thorough elaboration of detail. The overall picture of the 'life of the Earth' must make up for the lack of rigour in the individual inferences. A summary would therefore do Fechner an injustice.

(4) Riemann's plan: he will set aside Fechner's form of presentation and examine only the factual content. He will use the inductive method, that is, abstraction of general laws and their confirmation in explaining nature.

(5) The core argument begins with the question: from what do we infer that a body is ensouled, i.e. that a thought process takes place in it?
- We are immediately certain of our own ensoulment.
- For other beings (humans, animals) we infer it from individual purposive movements.
- Wherever we trace perceived purposiveness to a cause, we place that cause in a thought process; we have no other mode of explanation.
- Riemann takes thinking to be a process in ponderable matter. Yet the impossibility of explaining thinking from motions of matter will be evident to anyone who examines inner perception without prejudice. For the argument he nonetheless grants the abstract possibility of such an explanation.
- Nobody denies that purposiveness is perceived on Earth. The only question is where to locate the thought process that causes it.

(6) Footnote: only conditional purposes are meant here, those occurring at definite times and periods. Unconditional purposes are explained by an eternal Willing, not one produced in a thought process.

(7) The next page continues with criteria for assigning a thought process to a body. These are that purposiveness should not already close off in the body's parts, and that there should be no reason to seek its cause in a larger whole. Riemann then argues that organic purposiveness points to a cause in a larger whole, the Earth.
errors: There are no mathematical errors, since there is no mathematics.

Possible philosophical tension: Riemann says he can regard thinking only as a process in ponderable matter, yet declares it impossible to explain thinking from motions of matter. He leaves this unresolved, provisionally granting the abstract possibility.
The question 'Fragen wir uns zunächst, woraus ... wir die Beseeltheit eines Körpers' is left syntactically incomplete. The verb 'schließen' is struck out and not replaced, apparently a drafting slip.

results.what: Methodological contrast between Fechner's argument by analogy (Earth compared with the human organism) and the inductive method of abstracting laws and testing them in explaining nature
results.modern_name: Critique of analogical argument in Naturphilosophie; inductive-hypothetical method
results.usually_credited_to: General 19th-century philosophy of science (Herschel, Mill); Fechner's own position from Nanna 1848 and Zend-Avesta 1851

results.what: Inference to other minds from purposive movements, and localisation of the cause of purposiveness in a thought process within a body, or in a larger whole such as the Earth
results.modern_name: Argument from analogy for other minds; teleological inference; panpsychist 'Earth soul' thesis
results.usually_credited_to: Fechner (Earth soul); argument from analogy for other minds (J. S. Mill and others)

results.what: Distinction between conditional (temporally bounded) purposes and unconditional purposes grounded in an eternal Will

deep.surprise_reason: Riemann's interest in Fechner and in the 'Erdseele' doctrine is well known. Philosophical fragments from his Nachlass, including discussions of Fechner and of mind and matter, were printed by Weber and Dedekind in the Gesammelte Werke as 'Fragmente philosophischen Inhalts'. This page appears to be a draft of, or related to, that material. It has no mathematical content.
transcription_corrections: 'Nanna' is correct. It is Fechner's 'Nanna oder über das Seelenleben der Pflanzen' (1848). 'Fechner' at the start is secure from context.
'jeder F. Ansicht' is more plausibly 'der F. Ansicht', i.e. 'der Fechner'schen Ansicht'.
In the margin, 'Körpers' is written above the struck-out 'Dinges'. The parenthesis reads approximately '(des Stattfindens eines Denkprozesses in ihm)'.
'Das Denken selbst aber können wir' may read 'kann ich' in the image; the line contains a struck-out 'im Innern'.
In 'das Denken aus Bewegungen', the word 'Bewegungen' appears struck out with a replacement written above. The replacement is uncertain and is not simply 'Bewegungen'.
'wahrgenommene Zweckmäßigkeit' is an interlinear replacement for the struck-out 'Zweckmäßigkeit'. 'Erklärungsart' has 'art' struck out, leaving 'Erklärung'.
The verb at the end of 'Es fragt sich nur, wohin wir den Denkprozeß ... zu verlegen haben' reads 'zu verlegen' (without 'haben'). The final 'Auf die Erde' is struck out.
The folio number '17' appears in the right margin.
